parts:
On 7/19/12 2:44 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> B
>
> I'll try some sims and see what happens. I am happy to have separate mass matrix and epsilon.
> I actually find it helpful to separate these. As Mike explained to me, we can roughly think of the
> mass matrix as corresponding to the variance of the target distribution (that's not really right
> in general but it makes sense in the simple case) and then it makes sense to have epsilon*L
> to be approx 1.

Just the separate mass matrix and epsilon are not
identified. So you can always reascale epsilon
and the mass matrix so that epsilon * L = 1 if you're
doing HMC. For NUTS, L isn't fixed, plus you sample
along the path, not just at the end.

I'd like to know what's special about 1 here. NUTS II tries
to find an epsilon that works best for ALL params in terms
of achieving a 65% accept rate, then it fits a diagonal
mass matrix around that. So I don't see why you'd wind
up with epsilon * L = 1 as a result.

My understanding is that if epsilon * L = 1, the
exact balance between epsilon and L involves
balancing so that L is small and epsilon is large for
efficient movement with epsilon being small enough for
accurate Hamiltonian simulation.

> That's what you're getting: you have epsilon*L as about 6, which isn't
> far from the scale of most of the parameters in the model.
>
> Regarding the point at the end of your email, I'd be even happier if, instead of restarting a chain, we continued it at its current value with better tuning parameters. If that doesn't work, we can restart. But changing tuning parameters without changing the position would be cleaner.

We would be, too. We only do this when we
can't continue the current value because it's NaN or
+/- infinity. Once that's happen, there's no way to
get out of the hole through addition and multiplication.

I suppose we could go back to the initial values
and try again instead of regenerating those, too, but
often the problem is a poor (very low probability,
highly curved space) choice of starting point.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: 8schools!?!?!?!? + epsilon/mass + epsilon*L = 1
parts:
> Just the separate mass matrix and epsilon are not
> identified. So you can always reascale epsilon
> and the mass matrix so that epsilon * L = 1 if you're
> doing HMC. For NUTS, L isn't fixed, plus you sample
> along the path, not just at the end.

I would argue that the step size and the mass matrix are NOT
non-identified, even in regular HMC. In the limit \epilson -> 0 that
might be true, but when \epsilon is non-zero you have to worry about
the momenta update,
a la p += -\epsilon * gradV (notice the mass matrix doesn't show up
here). If \epsilon is too large then the update can be unstable, and
there's no mass matrix small enough to suppress that instability (you
know, other than zero).

(Matt and I have discussed this before. He's in Bob's camp, but I'm
pretty sure the finite step size case is not the same as the ideal
case).

> I'd like to know what's special about 1 here. NUTS II tries
> to find an epsilon that works best for ALL params in terms
> of achieving a 65% accept rate, then it fits a diagonal
> mass matrix around that. So I don't see why you'd wind
> up with epsilon * L = 1 as a result.

If you've successfully standardized your distribution then it should
look like a standardized gaussian, where the width of the typical set
is about 1. In that case the optimal distance to travel is 1 =
\epsilon * L.

I didn't even know there were camps! I thought

section 5.4.2.4 in Radford's handbook paper,
where he concludes they're equivalent,
I see that he modifies the epsilons on the
p updates so that they are parameter dependent:

p[i] += - epsilon[i] * gradV[i]

He then concludes that the resulting position/momentum
values "can no longer be interpreted as following Hamiltonian
dynamics at consistent time points" and goes on to
say "but that is of no consequence for the use of these
trajectories in HMC".

mass-based physical update, which takes

p[i] += epsilon * gradV[i]

I'm guessing Matt was talking about Radford's, so you
were considering different definitions of varying step
size.

Now I'll have to dive into our code to see what NUTS is
actually doing, having not recognized this distinction earlier.

> look like a standardized gaussian, where the width of the typical set
> is about 1. In that case the optimal distance to travel is 1 =
> \epsilon * L.

But isn't epsilon * L equal to time, not distance traveled?
With fixed epsilon and L, distance traveled has to depend on
the initial position and initial random momentum.

- Bob

Extreme mass matrices lead to large momenta which must be suppressed by the multiplication by the mass matrix upon the position updates. If we had infinite precision computers then the two approaches would give the same results, but on finite precision machines you can encounter adding/subtracting large numbers. I think the bigger issue, however, is that the large momenta updates can pass the stability threshold and cause the trajectory to diverge.

The mathematical question is whether or not the stability threshold scales with the mass matrix or not. That's probably a better definition of our camps. :-)

> But isn't epsilon * L equal to time, not distance traveled?
> With fixed epsilon and L, distance traveled has to depend on
> the initial position and initial random momentum.

Ah, but remember that the average magnitude of the momentum is the square root of the dimension, which is order unity, and 1*1=1.  In RMHMC the idea is that the more complicated momenta distribution helps to compensate so that the total distance traveled is just right for any distribution.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] varying epsilon vs. mass matrix & epsilon * L
parts:
NUTS is using the Radford-style parameter-specific step sizes, which
produces discretized dynamics for the positions (and the energy of the
momenta) that are equivalent to using a diagonal mass matrix with
appropriate variances, which is equivalent to transforming the space
that the variables live in to (hopefully) look more like a standard
normal.

I am pretty much 100% confident that the overall scale of the inverse
mass matrix and the squared step size are completely interchangeable
in the sense that scaling the inverse mass matrix by c and the step
size by 1/sqrt(c) will produce no change in the discretized dynamics
of the position vector or the energy of the momentum vector. (The
momenta will be different, but they'll have the same energy.)

If I may be pedantic, the width of the typical set of a standard
normal is more like 4 or 6 than 1. To continue to be (slightly less)
pedantic, if you've really transformed things so that you're working
with a standard normal, then I'm not sure that you really want to
always travel for epsilon*L=size of typical set, since you may hit a
weird resonance.

Matt

P.S. here's the silly function I wrote to compute split R-hat. I don't have the new n_eff, though; I'm waiting on all of you to create that!

monitor.split <- function (a){
dims <- dim(a)
n <- dims[1]
m <- dims[2]
a1 <- a[1:(n/2),,]
a2 <- a[(n/2+1):n,,]
dims.fat <- c(n/2,2*m,dims[3])
a.fat <- array (NA, dims.fat)
dimnames (a.fat) <- dimnames(a)
a.fat[,1:m,] <- a1
a.fat[,(m+1):(2*m),] <- a2
return (monitor (a.fat))
}

I seem to recall two contexts. One is to lower epsilon to get
a reasonable acceptance rate in all parts of the density and the
other is to avoid periodicities.

It's so cool that NUTS just does all this for us!

We're within epsilon of the BUGS estimates on all of

What's worrying is that it seems to be biased, not just noisy.
